title: Federal Workers Face Capped Top Ratings as Tougher Reviews Roll Out
excerpt: A new forced-distribution system limits ratings of 4 or 5 to 40% of staff, puts senior panels in charge of calibration, and leaves managers and employees warning of a hit to morale.
body:
• Federal employees are being rated for fiscal 2026 under a new forced-distribution system that caps top scores — a rating of 4 or 5 — at no more than 40% of General Schedule staff at each agency.
  • The second-lowest rating has been eliminated, shrinking the scale from five levels to four, and managers can now issue the lowest "unacceptable" rating without the higher-level review that was previously required.
  • Senior-executive calibration panels can reweight managers' proposed ratings behind closed doors, and employees say they have been given little information about the criteria being used.
  • Reader utility: your FY2026 rating affects awards and counts ahead of tenure in reduction-in-force retention rankings — HHS staff can request reconsideration within five business days of a final rating, and FEMA staff will be notified in December.

Federal agencies have begun rating employees for fiscal 2026, which ended on September 30, under the toughest performance system in decades — one that ranks workers against each other, caps the number of top scores, and, according to employees interviewed by Bloomberg Law and Government Executive, is already damaging morale.

For the first time in decades, federal employees will be ranked among their peers rather than evaluated solely against fixed performance standards, Bloomberg Law reported on October 20. The Office of Personnel Management finalised regulations in July that removed a longstanding ban on forced distribution, effective August 6. In September, OPM directed agencies to limit "outstanding" scores of five and "exceeds fully successful" scores of four to no more than 40% of their General Schedule employees in this year's cycle, according to Government Executive.

How the new system works

Under the previous system, about two-thirds of employees were rated beyond expectations, according to OPM data cited by Bloomberg Law. A 2013 GAO report found 99% of rank-and-file staff rated at or above "fully successful." OPM Director Scott Kupor has called those numbers not credible.

The system rests on that 40% cap, with about 60% of the bonus pool allocated to the top group, Kupor told Bloomberg Law. Agencies use "calibration boards" — senior-executive panels, sometimes as few as three people — to reweight managers' ratings to meet the distribution. The rule also eliminates the Level 2 rating and the higher-level review previously required for a Level 1 "unacceptable" rating, and bars rating challenges through union grievances once current agreements expire.

"There is a small group of people who tend to go above and beyond. If you want to attract high-performing people, they want to be in an environment where, when they distinguish themselves, they are recognized, rewarded, and promoted."

— Scott Kupor, Director, Office of Personnel Management

Managers squeezed, employees in the dark

The rollout has put managers in an awkward position. A manager at the Department of Veterans Affairs told Government Executive that four of his five direct reports had "quantifiably achieved at least a 4, but I'm not allowed to give them all a final rating that high." An IRS manager said a score of three was now expected "across the board," adding: "I'm sick of this constant abuse on good employees. Morale is low — really low."

At the Department of Health and Human Services, managers received calibration rubrics with instructions not to share preliminary scores, according to documents obtained by both outlets. FDA staff had until October 16 to submit self-assessments, but some received guidance only days before the deadline. At FEMA, final ratings will be set by November 20, with employees notified in December.

Why critics say the model backfires

Stacked ranking was popularised by General Electric in the 1980s and adopted by Microsoft in the 1990s, but Microsoft abandoned it in 2013, saying it warped incentives and discouraged teamwork. Herman Aguinis of George Washington University told Bloomberg Law that very few companies use it now because "the measures are so bad that the rankings are not easy to defend." Peter Cappelli of Wharton said ranked systems create a mindset in which "it's not in my interest to help you."

The AFGE local representing CDC headquarters staff called the rollout "a rushed and complicated system" that risks turning teammates into "competitors for limited recognition." At the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the National Treasury Employees Union plans a grievance, and unions have sued OPM over related appraisal rules.

What it means if you work for the federal government

The stakes are higher than a smaller bonus. Top scores bring cash and time-off awards, while low scores can make removal easier — and OPM's separate reduction-in-force rule now weights recent ratings ahead of tenure in retention rankings. For Indian Americans and immigrants in federal agencies and public-health institutions, the steps are immediate: keep a dated record of accomplishments before ratings are finalised, and use your agency's reconsideration window — five business days at HHS — if a final rating does not match the evidence. Agencies must comply by January 1, 2027.
